questions.prompt: What is the most accurate way to use the three broad vocal categories?

options.text: As a dictionary that assigns one reliable meaning to each sound family.
options.feedback: The categories describe broad sound forms and typical contexts. They do not turn a particular meow or purr into a fixed translation.

options.text: As vocabulary to combine with body language, location, routine, and recent events.
options.feedback: This is the best answer because it preserves the information in the sound while keeping interpretation dependent on other available channels.

options.text: Only hostile sounds carry usable information; murmurs and meows should be ignored.
options.feedback: All three categories carry communication information. The limitation concerns exact interpretation from an isolated cue, not whether the cue exists.

questions.prompt: Why is scratching relevant to a chapter about communication?

options.text: It leaves both a visible mark and a chemical mark from paw glands along travelled routes.
options.feedback: This is the best answer. Scratching has a dual visual and scent-marking function and belongs in the communication picture.

options.text: It is mainly a deliberate warning directed at whichever person owns the marked furniture.
options.feedback: The evidence does not support a spiteful person-directed message. The marking behaviour is species-typical and tied to place and identity.

options.text: It has no communication role unless urine marking occurs in the same location.
options.feedback: Scratching carries its own visible and chemical information. It does not require a second marking channel to become meaningful.

questions.prompt: What did the registered meow study show about human listeners?

options.text: Experienced owners could identify each meow's exact context with high reliability.
options.feedback: Owners were only modestly more accurate in some contexts, and specific context classification did not rise meaningfully above chance overall.

options.text: Specific context was difficult to identify from sound alone, though broad emotional valence was sometimes sensed.
options.feedback: This is the best answer and keeps the distinction between exact context classification and broad positive or negative valence.

options.text: Meows carry no information and should not influence an owner's observation.
options.feedback: The study removed context and did not show that meows are meaningless. It supports combining the sound with information available in real life.

questions.prompt: Which statement accurately represents the source limitation for the meow study?

options.text: It tested ten Maine Coon cats and deliberately removed situational and visual context.
options.feedback: This is the best answer. The small single-breed sample and listener-only design narrow what can responsibly be concluded.

options.text: It studied every major breed in normal homes while owners watched body language.
options.feedback: That would be a very different design. The registered study used a small single-breed sample and isolated recordings.

options.text: Its main limitation is that participants were all people who had never lived with cats.
options.feedback: The sample included owners and non-owners. Ownership produced only a modest advantage in some contexts, not an absent comparison group.

questions.prompt: Milo yowls at the door near dinner time. Which first action uses the combined-reading method?

options.text: Open the door because the location gives the yowl a specific meaning.
options.feedback: Location is one useful fact, but acting immediately still lets a single interpretation outrun body language, routine, and what Milo does next.

options.text: Check her orientation, ears, tail, feeding routine, recent events, and next movement.
options.feedback: This is the best action because it combines the vocal cue with body language and situational evidence before choosing a response.

options.text: Ignore the yowl so Milo does not learn that sound controls household decisions.
options.feedback: This removes a real channel instead of interpreting it carefully. Uncertainty calls for more observation, not automatic dismissal.

questions.prompt: A housemate missed Milo's pacing episode. What information best supports a retrospective judgement?

options.text: Whichever eyewitness gives the most confident and detailed interpretation.
options.feedback: Detail can help, but confidence is not accuracy. The missing channels should be reconstructed from observations rather than personality.

options.text: The shared log's time and routine details plus specific questions about Milo's body language.
options.feedback: This is the best response because it restores recorded context and separates observable details from competing explanations.

options.text: No information, because an event that cannot be watched live can no longer be interpreted responsibly.
options.feedback: The conclusion may remain limited, but a dated observation record exists precisely to preserve context after the moment has passed.

questions.prompt: A sound, posture, and context point in different directions. What is the most responsible conclusion?

options.text: Choose the loudest or most dramatic cue because it is least likely to be accidental.
options.feedback: Salience does not establish meaning. A dramatic sound can still be ambiguous when the other channels and situation do not agree.

options.text: Keep the interpretation provisional, gather another observation, and avoid a high-consequence action meanwhile.
options.feedback: This is the best synthesis. Combined reading improves judgement but is allowed to end in uncertainty rather than manufactured confidence.

options.text: Average the cues into a neutral interpretation and assume no response is ever needed.
options.feedback: The method is not numerical averaging, and uncertainty does not always mean inaction. It means matching the next step to the evidence and stakes.
